thread.title: As the U.S.-China trade war starts to heat up, here’s the next step for investors - MarketWatch

author: Barbara Kollmeyer
title: As the U.S.-China trade war starts to heat up, here’s the next step for investors - MarketWatch
text:
They’ve got us by the beans. Soybeans, that is.
So much for those US 'consumer neutral' #tariffs . My guess is US #soybean producers aren't that happy with #Trump now. Soybean prices down 5%. pic.twitter.com/jbkaMXqS4Y
— jeroen blokland (@jsblokland) April 4, 2018 With U.S. investors barely out of bed, China lowered the tariff boom on 106 American products — a bummer for tofu lovers and a whole lot more. So, the risk-off playbook has been whisked out, as equities bleed red from sea to shining sea and gold climbs. Beijing’s move came less than 24 hours after 1,300 of its own products got hit by U.S. levies.
Outside of soybeans, collateral damage is hitting Boeing BA, +2.60% and Ford F, +2.67% — airplanes, SUVs and trucks are all on Beijing’s hit list, along with whiskey, beef and corn. Plus, techs are going along for another hard ride down, as worries build about where this trade mess goes next.
“Most analysts and investors still assume a last-minute deal can avert tariffs actually being imposed. Maybe. But by then damage may already have been done. And neither Trump nor Xi can afford to appear to back down and look weak in front of a domestic audience,” says energy analyst John Kemp in a tweet.
Guys, I'm starting to worry about Trump. I know, he's all about "Art of the Deal", but he's doing some real damage?
— Paul Theron (@paul_vestact) April 4, 2018 Clearly the market has been holding its breath for a trade nightmare, which brings us to our call of the day . Jasper Lawler, head of research at LGC, explains why investors are understandably freaked out by this latest development.
“There is more room to the downside for equities, because investors are second-guessing the initial belief that this can be wrapped up in a civilized way without the need for tariffs,” he says in emailed comments
If there is any bright note to this stupid nonsense it's we will bottom quickly. https://t.co/wiyVzCLaFe
— BamaBull (@Bamabroker) April 4, 2018 But Lawler has this solid piece of advice for equity investors as they brace yet another for a bumpy ride.
“Timing exits and entries in these volatile markets is a tough ask for retail investors. The best move is probably to stick it out, if you believe this can blow over once the focus shifts to strong company earnings,” he says.
We are just days away from earnings season, and there’s at least some optimism on that front.
Key market gauges The Dow is looking at a more-than-400-point starting drop, with futures for the blue-chip index, YMM8, -2.10% , the S&P 500 ESM8, -1.61% and Nasdaq NQM8, -1.89% deep in the red. European stocks SXXP, -1.05% are getting hit fairly hard, too , while Asian stocks closed lower, but before China announced its tariff list.
The dollar DXY, -0.13% is down , notably against the yen USDJPY, -0.41% . Crude CLM8, -1.53% has tanked alongside stock futures, down nearly 2%, with U.S. supply data due later.
Not to be left out, bitcoin BTCUSD, -5.10% is down nearly 5%, and other cryptos are also under pressure.
See the Market Snapshot column for the latest action.
The chart Lots of dramatic chart action went down as China hit markets with that tariff news. Gold GCM8, +0.79% is still steaming ahead this morning, as it scoops up safe-haven bids .
Gold pops UBS’s global chief investment officer, Mark Haefele, had a bit more to say about safe havens in a note that came out before the China news hit. He urged investors not to flee, but suggested adding some protection against stock-market turmoil via 10-year Treasury bonds and the Japanese yen.
The buzz High-flying cloud company Cloudera CLDR, +4.76% is taking a hit after posting upbeat results, but putting out a sharply lower outlook for fiscal 2019 — something that may give already nervous investors pause .
WPP WPP, +0.36% WPP, -1.97% is under pressure on news the ad giant’s board is probing Chief Executive Martin Sorrell over finances and an allegation of personal misconduct.
Apple AAPL, +1.03% has hired its first senior vice president of artificial intelligence . It’s tapped John Giannandrea, who left a similar role at Alphabet-owned Google GOOGL, +0.60% earlier this week.
CBS CBS, +4.24% has made a bid for Viacom VIA, -6.19% VIAB, -3.70% but wants its management to be at the helm, say sources. The all-stock offer is below Viacom’s current market valuation.
The Quote: “Those who attempt to make China surrender through pressure or intimidation have never succeeded before, and will not succeed now.” — China’s Foreign Ministry spokesman Geng Shuang talks to reporters after the country revealed its retaliatory tariffs.
The economy A fairly busy data day is ahead, kicking off with ADP employment report for March, which comes ahead of Friday’s big jobs data . Updates on the Markit services purchasing managers’ index, the Institute for Supply Management’s nonmanufacturing index and factory orders are all out today. We’ll also have the minutes from the most recent Fed meeting.
Check out: MarketWatch’s Economic Calendar
The stat $200 — That’s how much more Americans paid in 2017 compared to the year prior to buy a basket of vice goods, such as drugs, booze and cigarettes, according to the annual Bloomberg Global Vice Index .
The gauge, which covers 100 countries, shows how much of an individual’s income is needed to keep up a weekly habit of those not-so-great-for-you items. And for three-fours of those countries, bad habits eat up one-third of average weekly paychecks. Ukrainians pay the most for vice goods, while they are cheapest in Luxembourg, the index shows.
